lessons.subject: Civic Education
lessons.title: What civic education means, and the right, the responsibility and the informed part of taking part
objectives: State a working definition of civic education in your own words and name the two civic-education institutions that description rests on.
Tell a right apart from a responsibility in three everyday school and community situations, and give one of each for each situation.
Describe informed participation in a decision as two actions a teacher can see, and use both on a case.
lessons.body:
WHAT CIVIC EDUCATION MEANS, AND THE THREE IDEAS A DEFINITION OF IT CARRIES

What you will learn: one workable definition of civic education and its source; how a right differs from a responsibility in situations a pupil actually meets; and what someone does differently when they join a decision informed.

This lesson teaches the meaning part of the first week of the scheme. The other three sections of that week are not taught here and the week is not reported as complete. It carries content approval PENDING and verification DEFERRED: material offered to a teacher, not a certified lesson.

1. THE DEFINITION, AND THE TWO INSTITUTIONS BEHIND IT
Civic education is the part of schooling that teaches how public life is arranged and what a person owes it: the rules a community runs itself by, the claims each member can make on that community, and the claims the community makes in return. It is built from two institutions, not from this lesson's opinion.
The first is Nigeria's curriculum authority, the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council. In its Executive Secretary's address to the January 2019 workshop reviewing the senior secondary Civic Education curriculum, the Council treats the subject as building the skills and competencies tied to social norms and values, says that it stresses the "rights, roles and duties of members of the society", and puts its goal as "the development of responsible citizenship"; at this level, it adds, the subject should make clear how citizens, government and society relate and what each side owes the other.
The second is the UNICEF research office in Innocenti. The section headed "What is civic education?" in its explainer on the subject says that in its simplest form civic education teaches how political institutions and processes work and what citizens' rights and responsibilities are, and that it reaches on into how government works, how elections are run, the rule of law and how decisions are taken. The same section notes that the field holds many definitions and imposes no single standard one, and it argues that taking part well today also needs critical thinking and the ability to judge information - so this lesson treats being informed as part of the subject, not as preparation for it.
The two authorities differ in wording, not in content: what a person may claim, what a person owes, and how the decisions that affect both are made and entered.

2. A RIGHT AND A RESPONSIBILITY ARE ONE ARRANGEMENT SEEN FROM EACH SIDE
A right is a claim a person may make on the arrangement simply because they belong to it - not a reward for conduct and not a favour. A responsibility is what the arrangement needs back from that person. Drop the second and the first becomes a privilege for whoever speaks loudest. Three everyday cases, none of them partisan:
Class reading corner. Right: any pupil whose turn is on the rota may borrow a shared book for the listed period. Responsibility: the book returns to its shelf in the state it left. Informed participation: before the class votes on a new borrowing rule, a pupil reads the rule as written on the draft notice instead of arguing with what they suppose the teacher intends.
Notice about the community water point. Right: a household on the scheme list gets its turn at the tap. Responsibility: the tap is left ready for the next household and a broken handle is reported rather than forced. Informed participation: before repeating what the notice says, the pupil checks it against the notice itself and against whoever maintains the point - two sources, not the first voice.
Rumour of a new school charge. Right: a pupil and their family may ask what is charged and by whom. Responsibility: the question goes to the office that issues the charge rather than to a forwarded message. Informed participation: find out what the paper says and whom it affects before taking a side.

3. INFORMED PARTICIPATION, IN TWO MOVES
Move one is finding out what is actually proposed and whom it affects. Move two is checking whether what you know comes from the thing itself - the notice, the draft rule, the announcement - or only from a message about it. Both are actions a teacher can see, so both can be marked.

4. WHAT THIS LESSON DOES NOT SAY
It names no party, candidate, association or group and prefers none: it teaches the arrangement, not a side. It states nothing about Nigerian law or the powers of any office - no source used here is a legal text, and the accuracy of any such claim belongs to CIV-FACT-T1-CITIZENSHIP-LAW, CIV-FACT-T1-GOVERNMENT-STRUCTURE and CIV-FACT-T1-SELF-DEFENCE-LAW. It copies none of the scheme's sentences on this topic: the two definition lines of the week are cited by number only, and one of them describes pupils in terms of following, which this lesson neither repeats nor endorses. Which definition the class is taught - the scheme's first line, its second, both, or this supplement - is a teacher's decision, recorded as CIVIC-EDUCATION-T1-W01-MEANING-DEFINITION-CHOICE and not settled here.

5. WHERE THE SCHEME STANDS
The scheme puts this week's content as meaning and needs in one line (scheme line 13) and states two definitions in the two body paragraphs under the topic heading (lines 127 and 129), with no heading over either. Their digests are held in the queue record so a reader can find those exact lines in the source. Two things to know before teaching from them: the words participate and informed occur nowhere in this scheme document, so the third idea of this lesson is not the scheme's wording and is not offered as its finding; the words rights and responsibilities do occur, which is why those two ideas are common ground.

6. WHAT IS STILL MISSING
The week's other three blocks - the needs list at lines 131 to 141, the school-level list at 143 to 157 and the nation-building list at 159 to 171 - are not taught here and stay unmapped. The scheme prints no question, answer, mark or rubric in Week 1, so the three exercises below are proposals awaiting the teacher; no source key exists to check them against. Package status, the three term-alias approvals and the neutral-teaching gate all remain as they were.

practice.question: Say what civic education is in your own words, and name the two institutions whose account of the subject this lesson rests on.
practice.answer: Civic education is the part of schooling that teaches how public life is arranged and what a person owes it - the rules a community runs itself by, the claims each member can make on it, and the claims it makes in return. The two institutions are the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council, whose 2019 review address treats the subject as building skills and competencies tied to social norms and values, stresses the rights, roles and duties of members of society, and gives its goal as responsible citizenship; and the UNICEF research office in Innocenti, whose explainer says that in its simplest form the subject teaches how political institutions and processes work and what citizens' rights and responsibilities are, extending to how government works, how elections are run, the rule of law and the way decisions are taken.

marking.criterion: Gives the definition in the pupil's own words rather than copying a line of this lesson or of the scheme
Carries both halves of the arrangement - what a member may claim and what a member owes
Names the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council as the curriculum authority
Names the UNICEF research office in Innocenti as the second account

practice.question: Take the class reading corner and the community water point. For each, name one right and one responsibility, and say which arrangement each one keeps.
practice.answer: Reading corner: the right is that any pupil whose turn is on the rota may borrow a shared book for the listed period, and it keeps the arrangement that the corner is open to the whole class rather than to the quickest hand; the responsibility is that the book goes back to its shelf in the state it left, and it keeps the same arrangement usable for the next pupil. Water point: the right is that a household on the scheme list gets its turn at the tap, which keeps the agreed order of service; the responsibility is that the tap is left ready for the next household and a fault is reported instead of forced, which keeps the supply and the order standing. In both cases the right and the responsibility are the same arrangement seen from each side, and neither works without the other.

marking.criterion: Says for each pair what the arrangement it keeps is, instead of listing the pair

practice.question: A message is going round the class about a change to the timetable that no one has seen. Using the two moves of informed participation, say what a pupil should do before taking a side, and name the right and the responsibility in the case.
practice.answer: Move one: find out what is actually proposed and whom it affects - read the notice or the draft timetable itself, and ask which classes the change touches, rather than arguing from the message. Move two: check the source of what they know, so the claim is confirmed against the thing issued (the office copy, the posted notice) or against a second person who has seen it, not carried on because one message arrived first. The right is that a pupil and their family may ask what is proposed and on what authority before it is applied to them. The responsibility is to answer from what the paper says rather than from the rumour, and to let the class hear the same checked information instead of two versions. A pupil who does both moves may still disagree with the change; what differs is that they now know what they are disagreeing with.

marking.criterion: States move one - what is proposed and whom it affects
States move two - checking against the thing issued or a second source, applied to this case
Names a right that fits the case
Names a responsibility that fits the case
